lead: Probability starts with events; most questions ask for a number attached to an event, such as a payment amount or a count of failures. A random variable turns each outcome into a real number, so you can add, compare and integrate. Discrete variables count; continuous variables measure. Their pmf, pdf and CDF answer the same question in three forms: how much probability sits at a value, over an interval, or up to a point. This chapter builds those tools; later units use them for named distributions, expectations and tests.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for events and axioms, and basic integration for continuous densities.

blocks.text: A random variable X is a function X: Ω → ℝ. Ω is the sample space, the set of all outcomes; ω is one outcome; X(ω) is the real number assigned to it. Example: roll a die, Ω={1,...,6}; X(ω)=ω. Or a UPI payment: the outcome is a transaction record; X is its amount in rupees.

A discrete random variable has possible values in a finite or countably infinite set, such as 0,1,2,... failures. A continuous random variable has possible values filling an interval, such as time until a Chennai power cut ends, in minutes. Often the question states the type; if not, decide from the support — a list of separate values means discrete, an interval means continuous.

The support is the smallest set that carries all probability. For discrete X, support is values x with p(x)>0. For continuous X, support is where f(x)>0; endpoints do not matter because single points have probability 0. Write support explicitly: f(x)=2x for 0≤x≤1 and f(x)=0 otherwise. Without the “otherwise” the density is incomplete.

sections.h3: pmf and pdf: probability at a value or over an interval

blocks.text: For discrete X the probability mass function (pmf) is p(x)=P(X=x). p(x) is the probability that X equals x; it is a number from 0 to 1. Two conditions: p(x)≥0 for every x, and Σ p(x)=1, sum over support. Then P(X∈A)=Σ p(x) for x in A. For a fair die, p(k)=1/6 for k=1,...,6; the sum is 1.

blocks.where: p(x) is the probability mass at value x; the sum runs over all support values of X.

blocks.text: For continuous X the probability density function (pdf) f(x) gives probability by area, not by height. Conditions: f(x)≥0 for all x, and ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over all real x. For any interval, P(a<X≤b)=∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. The probability at a single point is zero: P(X=x)=0. So P(a<X≤b)=P(a≤X≤b)=P(a<X<b). A pdf value can exceed 1; f(0.9)=1.8 in f(x)=2x is allowed because an interval of tiny width carries a small area.

blocks.where: f(x) is the probability density; the integral is the area under f from a to b. The total area over all real x is 1.

blocks.text: Some syllabi say probability mass function for pmf and probability density function for pdf; a few call the pmf a discrete density. Keep the symbols: p for mass, f for density. Use p with sums and f with integrals. Mixing them is the commonest error.

sections.h3: CDF and the link to pmf or pdf

blocks.text: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is F(x)=P(X≤x), for both discrete and continuous X. F(x) is the probability that X is at most x. It uses ≤; the value at x includes x. For any a<b, P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a). This interval formula is the safest way to use a CDF. Some syllabi call F the distribution function.
F(x) = P(X ≤ x),   P(a < X ≤ b) = F(b) − F(a)
blocks.where: F(x) is the CDF at x; a and b are real numbers with a < b.

items: F is nondecreasing: if x₁<x₂ then F(x₁)≤F(x₂).
F is right-continuous: the limit from the right, F(x+)=lim over h→0⁺ of F(x+h), equals F(x).
F(x)→0 as x→−∞ and F(x)→1 as x→∞.

blocks.text: For continuous X, F(x)=∫ from −∞ to x of f(t) dt. Where F is differentiable, f(x)=F′(x). The CDF removes the interval issue: P(0.2<X≤0.6)=F(0.6)−F(0.2). In the figure, F(x)=x², so the probability is 0.36−0.04=0.32.

For discrete X, F is a step function: F(x)=Σ p(t) for t≤x. It is flat between support values and jumps at each support value x by p(x). Example: p(0)=0.2, p(1)=0.5, p(2)=0.3 gives F(x)=0 for x<0; 0.2 for 0≤x<1; 0.7 for 1≤x<2; 1 for x≥2. At a jump the CDF takes the upper value because of ≤.

figure.caption: For f(x)=2x on (0,1), F(x)=x². The area under f from 0 to 0.6 is 0.36, so P(0.2<X≤0.6)=0.36−0.04=0.32.

spec.aria: Plot from x = 0 to 1 of the density f(x) = 2x and the CDF F(x) = x²; the area under f up to 0.6 is 0.36.

examples.question: A continuous random variable X has pdf f(x)=2x for 0≤x≤1, and f(x)=0 otherwise. Find the CDF F(x) and P(0.2<X≤0.6).
steps: Check that f is valid: ∫₀¹ 2x dx = [x²]₀¹ = 1, so total area is 1.
For x<0, F(x)=P(X≤x)=0 because the density is zero below 0.
For x>1, F(x)=1 because all probability is below 1.
examples.answer: The CDF is F(x)=0 for x less than 0; F(x)=x² for 0≤x≤1; F(x)=1 for x greater than 1. The probability P(0.2 < X ≤ 0.6)=0.32 (unitless).
examples.check:
F06 = round(0.6**2, 2)
F02 = round(0.2**2, 2)
print(F06)
print(F02)
print(round(F06 - F02, 2))

traps: A pdf value is not a probability; f(x) can exceed 1. Probability is area over an interval, and P(X=x)=0 for continuous X.
Use intervals for continuous X. Asking for P(X=0.5) gives 0, not f(0.5).
The CDF uses ≤: P(a<X≤b)=F(b)−F(a). For discrete X, P(a≤X≤b) needs F(b)−F(a−) or p(a) added.
Always state the support. f(x)=2x alone is incomplete; it needs 0≤x≤1 and zero otherwise. Likewise the pmf sums only over support.
Do not mix sums and integrals: pmf uses Σ p(x)=1, pdf uses ∫ f(x) dx=1. A “density” can mean pdf, not pmf.

quiz.q: Define a random variable and write its mapping X: Ω → ℝ, naming Ω and ω.
quiz.a: A random variable is a function X: Ω → ℝ from sample space Ω to real numbers; each outcome ω maps to X(ω).

quiz.q: State the two conditions for a pmf p(x).
quiz.a: p(x)≥0 for all x, and Σ p(x)=1 over the support.

quiz.q: Why is P(X=x)=0 for a continuous random variable with pdf f?
quiz.a: Probability is area under f; a single point has zero width, so ∫ from x to x of f(t)dt=0. For continuous X, probability lives in intervals.

quiz.q: X has pdf f(x)=c x² for 0<x<1, zero otherwise. Find c.
quiz.a: ∫₀¹ c x² dx = c/3 = 1, so c=3.

quiz.q: For F(x)=x² on [0,1] (0 below, 1 above), find P(0.2<X≤0.6).
Explain why the CDF of a discrete variable is a step function and what the jump size at x is.
quiz.a: F sums p(t) for t≤x; between support values no new mass is added, so F is flat; at a support value it jumps by p(x).

quiz.q: For f(x)=2x on (0,1), f(0.9)=1.8. Why is this not a contradiction with f being a density?
quiz.a: Density is height, not probability; probability is area. A narrow interval around 0.9 has area about 1.8×width, still ≤1 if width is small. Conditions are f≥0 and total area 1, not f≤1.

beyond: Not for the exam. The CDF is the main object in simulation: if U is uniform on [0,1], then X=F⁻¹(U) has CDF F. This inverse transform sampling powers Monte Carlo in finance and physics. In survival analysis, the CDF of a lifetime is replaced by a survival function 1−F. In machine learning, density estimation learns f or F from data. Search next for “probability integral transform”, “quantile function” and “kernel density estimation”.
